description: The Gemma 4 chat template: the byte string a conversation renders to before tokenization, shared by the training tier and the rust-harness prompt builders

notes.version_lockstep: chat_template_version is CHAT_TEMPLATE_VERSION on both sides. Version 2 corrected Gemma 4 from the Gemma 3 <start_of_turn>/<end_of_turn> framing. A prepared SFT dataset records the version in its manifest and training/data/sft.py refuses a stale one, so a template change invalidates stale artifacts rather than silently retraining against a different prompt.
notes.rendered_is_a_subset_of_markers: The tokenizer defines channel, tool-call, tool, and think markers that neither writer renders. The canonical template strips thought channels from history, and the harness carries a tool call as JSON inside a model turn. They appear here only so both sides neutralize the same set in untrusted content; emitting them would diverge from the training tier.
notes.neutralization_is_harness_only: neutralized_in_content is the harness's set, pinned exactly by rust-harness/harness/src/template.rs::MARKERS. The training tier renders trusted curated conversations and does not sanitize, so it has no counterpart to compare; the Python side asserts only that what it renders, and the thinking_markers it refuses in SFT sources, are covered here. bos is in the set because template.rs writes it as prompt text and generator::PROMPT_SPECIALS resolves that literal to the boundary id, so unneutralized content carrying it would start a second sequence.
notes.trim_content_follows_python: trim_content true means Python's str.strip, which trims by str.isspace. That set is the Unicode White_Space property plus the C0 separators U+001C-U+001F, so Rust's str::trim is not equivalent: template.rs trims with is_python_space instead. A tool result carrying a separator byte at a content edge is the reachable case, and the whitespace-edged fixture in template_contract.rs pins it against the real Python renderer.
notes.roles_are_not_comparable: The two tiers enumerate roles differently. Python takes a role string per message and maps only the assistant role through assistant_role. Rust maps its own Role enum, folding Tool onto user and Compaction onto system, because Transcript::effective folds compactions into System before rendering. The rendered turn framing is identical; the role vocabulary that reaches it is not.
notes.bos_placement: Python emits bos as the first segment of render_segments. Rust emits it from template::render and from each incremental prompt builder, because template::render is not on the harness prompt path. Both produce exactly one bos at offset 0.
notes.open_model_turn: Rust appends '<|turn>model\n' to a prompt to open the turn the model completes. Python renders closed conversations for training and never appends it, so a rendered-string comparison must stop at the last closed turn.
notes.canonical_template_is_the_authority: docs/models/gemma4-chat-template.jinja is Google's own template, extracted verbatim from tokenizer.chat_template in the E2B and E4B GGUF metadata (byte-identical across both). The marker and spec values here are checked against it, so a marker no checkpoint defines now fails a test instead of tokenizing as a byte run.
notes.bos_is_a_variable_in_the_canonical_templ: The literal <bos> does not occur in the canonical template; it emits {{- bos_token -}} and the tokenizer resolves it (tokenizer.ggml.add_bos_token is also true in the GGUF metadata). spec.bos records the resolved string because both tiers write the literal into the prompt.
